description: We are a two-person team combining software development with a strong natural science background. We want to build a practical astronaut health monitoring system focused on meaningful health indicators, nutrition, metabolism, and clear data insights.
summary:
Bioskopos is a phone app that lets astronauts check their own health before, during and after a mission, and act on what they find. Three quick checks feed one health score from 0 to 100: a self check (questionnaire, a reaction game, a memory game and smartwatch data), a blood test and a urine test. The score is split into muscle, bone, hydration, mind and sleep, and immune health, colour-coded at a glance.

Each check sets its own rhythm: the further its values drift from their range, the more often it is due, from weekly down to daily. A clickable body map colours every area by its state, and pattern rules link off-range values and symptoms to known spaceflight risks from NASA's Human Research Program, such as kidney stones, space anemia, bone loss and SANS. Every blood marker is charted across the mission next to the real Inspiration4 crew from NASA's Open Science Data Repository, so an astronaut can see whether a change is normal for spaceflight or worth a call to the flight surgeon. Tips, on-board food suggestions and a private crew overview turn numbers into actions. All analysis runs on the device; no health data leaves it.
details:
Try it

Open https://bioskopos.vercel.app, tap the phone, choose "Explore the demo", pick Alex Morgan and enter PIN 0000. The panel next to the phone explains every screen. An Android build can be downloaded from the same page.

Our mission

Long missions to the Moon and Mars will take crews far beyond quick help from Earth. We want every astronaut to understand their own body during a mission: to notice early when something drifts, to know how serious it is, and to know what to do about it. Bioskopos turns a few short checks into one clear picture and concrete next steps, while the data stays with the astronaut.

Who we are

Team FFSP is two people from Austria with complementary backgrounds. Paul Walcher comes from the natural sciences and nutrition: he chose the health indicators, their target ranges and how they are weighted into the score, and he shaped the food and health advice. Phillip Lutz is a software developer: he designed and built the app, the Android version and the website. Together we combined the science of what to measure with an app that makes it quick to measure and easy to understand.

What it does

Bioskopos helps astronauts assess their own health before, during and after a mission, and tells them what to do next.

  • Three independent checks. A self check (12 questions, a reaction game, a sequence memory game, smartwatch data such as sleep, heart rate variability, resting heart rate, breathing rate, SpO2 and skin temperature), a blood test and a urine test. About 48 health indicators in total.
  • One health score (0-100), built from five domains weighted by our team's marker table: muscle 30, bone 25, hydration 20, mind and sleep 15, immune 10. Four bands: Excellent, Monitoring required, Elevated risk, Critical.
  • An adaptive rhythm. Each check is a satellite in an orbit on the home screen. The further its values drift from range, the further out it moves and the more often it is due: weekly, every 3 days, every 2 days, daily. During flight and the first two weeks after landing no check runs slower than every 3 days. The app prompts the astronaut when a check is due, so measurements become part of the mission routine.
  • A body map. Every body area is coloured by its state and can be tapped. Symptoms can be reported from a list or by tapping where it hurts, with a 1-10 severity.
  • Patterns. Rule-based detectors look at the last 7 days and link values plus symptoms to 13 known spaceflight problems, including dehydration, kidney stone risk, a starting infection, faster bone loss, SANS (fluid pressure on the eyes), space anemia, orthostatic intolerance, space motion sickness and sleep debt. Every pattern lists the signs that triggered it, so it can always be explained, and it points to a conversation with the flight surgeon, never a diagnosis.
  • Trends. Dynamic charts for the score, each domain and every marker, aligned by mission phase (before launch, flight, after landing) so missions of different length are comparable.
  • Tips and food. The most relevant next steps, sorted into food and drink, body, mind, sleep and medical. The food tab knows the on-board pantry and marks items as good today, go easy on, or running low.
  • Crew. Several astronauts share one device, each behind a PIN or fingerprint. Crew mates only see a coarse status and how to support each other today; values and symptoms stay private.
  • Environment. Live ISS position with the radiation zones ahead (South Atlantic Anomaly, polar regions), cabin temperature, CO2 and humidity linked to symptoms, and for Moon and Mars missions a to-scale route with distance and signal delay.

How NASA data is used

  • The reference crew in every blood chart is the real SpaceX Inspiration4 crew: complete blood count and comprehensive metabolic panel of all four crew members from NASA's Open Science Data Repository (OSD-569, OSD-575), sampled from 92 days before launch to 194 days after landing. An astronaut sees their own curve next to the Inspiration4 band and can tell "everyone drops here" from "this is me".
  • The score domains and the spaceflight patterns follow the hazards and risks mapped by NASA's Human Research Program: bone loss, kidney stones, SANS, immune changes, cardiovascular and behavioural health.
  • The self check names NASA's tested Astroskin biosensor garment (NTRS 20190000238) as a future source for its wearable values; today they come from a smartwatch or heart-rate strap.
  • Planet positions for Moon and Mars missions come from JPL's approximate planetary positions.

Benefits and intended impact

On the ISS a flight surgeon is a call away. On the way to Mars, a signal takes up to 20 minutes each way. Astronauts need a tool that does not just collect numbers but says how worried to be and what to do. Bioskopos keeps checks short, raises their frequency only when values drift, and turns findings into concrete actions. The same approach works for people in isolated places on Earth: Antarctic stations, submarines, expeditions, remote clinics.

Privacy and offline use

All analysis runs on the device. There is no server and no account; health data never leaves the phone. This matters in space, where connectivity is limited, and for medical data in general.

How we built it

React 19, TypeScript and Vite as one codebase; Capacitor for the Android app (Health Connect for watch data, fingerprint unlock, haptics); plain CSS; hosted on Vercel. The analysis (score, rhythm, trend projection, patterns) is a set of pure TypeScript functions that run on the device.

What makes it creative

The check rhythm adapts to the astronaut instead of following a fixed schedule, and the orbit makes that visible in one look. Each person is compared with a real astronaut crew, not only with Earth reference ranges. The name comes from Greek: bios (life) and skopos (watcher).

Factors we considered and limits

  • Which measurements are realistic in space: in flight only a small point-of-care blood panel and urine strips are practical, so lab-only markers are tracked on a slower rhythm.
  • Earth reference ranges can mislead in flight (fluid shift), which is why the Inspiration4 band is shown next to them.
  • Inspiration4 was a 3-day flight with four people, so the reference band is narrow; longer missions would need more crews.
  • The demo crew and its readings are generated; the Inspiration4 values and the ISS position are real. Target ranges, score weights and tips are a first draft and not medically reviewed. Bioskopos is a prototype, not a medical device.
